The turn of the century - the one that turned a hundred years ago, not the one currently in the process of turning - brought a plethora of new inventions and innovations to the world: the automobile, the assembly line, motorized flight and mass production. The period also produced a technology in which light was projected through a sequence of still photos on a celluloid strip, creating the illusion of motion. It was inevitable that those of the creative bent would use this nascent medium to document the brave new world of technology and industrialization, and eventually use it as a device to tell stories. Georges Melies' Le Voyage dans la Lune took the idea of flight to its illogical extreme. Later, Charlie Chaplin poked fun at industrialization in Modern Times. To directors such as Fritz Lang, a fitting metaphor for the growing mechanization of society was the robot. Throughout the history of film, the idea of man creating a machine in his own image has proved irresistible to screenwriters. In their numerous film appearances, robots have been portrayed as heroes, villains, tragic figures and comic relief, exhibiting varying degrees of humanity and self-awareness. Maria, the automaton from Lang's Metropolis, turned on her creator and freed her fellow workers, while Forbidden Planet's Robby the Robot was blindly obedient to his creator, Dr. Morbius. C-3PO of the Star Wars saga displayed human emotions such as fear and annoyance, the latter usually directed at his diminutive friend, R2-D2. Alien's android, Ash, and the original Terminator were instruments of evil, while Short Circuit's Number 5 displayed a childlike innocence after being zapped to life by a bolt of lightning. The latest addition to the pantheon of cinematic cyborgs is the Touchstone/Columbia co-production Bicentennial Man. Directed by Chris Columbus, the film is based on a short story by Isaac Asimov, who later expanded it into a novel, The Positronic Man, co-written by Robert Silverberg. In Nicholas Kazan's screenplay, a robot designed for domestic duties is delivered to the Martin family in a not-too-distant future. All are impressed with the android except the oldest daughter, who declares that robots are 'all the same.' It soon becomes evident, however, that 'Andrew' is not like other robots. Inexplicably, this particular Northam Robotics household model, number NDR-113, displays such decidedly human traits as curiosity, creativity and affection. Those tendencies are encouraged by the family patriarch, Richard Martin (Sam Neill), who teaches the robot lessons both philosophical and practical, making 14 • CINEFEX 81 Andrew's human side increasingly manifest. The robot's quest to become a real man - a journey that spans several generations in the lives of the Martin family - is eventually aided by former Northam Robotics employee Rupert Burns (Oliver Platt), who uses sophisticated animatronic and bio-medical technology to transform the android into a real human being. The story's two-hundred-year timespan would not only require visual effects to depict futuristic environments, but extensive makeups to suggest the aging of major characters. The former would be provided by Dream Quest Images, and the latter by Cannom Creations. But the film's central effects issue was how actor Robin Williams could be transformed into the robot Andrew - a task that fell to Steve Johnson and his crew at XFX. With Andrew featured in nearly every scene, and his quest for humanity at the core of the story, it was crucial that any approach to conceiving the character be carefully considered. Every idea posited seemed burdened with a substantial downside. The robot could be rendered digitally, for example - but that meant that, except for his voice, Williams would be essentially absent from the first two-thirds of the movie. Another approach was to fit the actor with a full robot suit; but the fact that much of Williams' facial and body expressions would be lost made that solution a risky one. Furthermore, both the studio and the director feared that encasing Williams in a robot suit would essentially negate the artistic and commercial value of featuring so big a star Surprisingly - considering that actors often chafe at the discomfort and limitations of wearing heavy makeup and creature effects - Williams himself was a great supporter of the full robot suit idea. "Robin wanted to wear a suit," Johnson recalled. "I think he wanted to stretch as an actor by seeing if he could make a tin can perform." A third idea was to have Williams wear a more subtle robotic makeup, an approach that would have raised the actor's visibility in the picture, but also would have made the transition from robot to man far less dramatic. "Chris believed that Robin could carry the performance with just makeup, playing a more android type of robot. But most of us, Robin included, felt that the film wouldn't make sense unless Andrew started out looking very mechanical. This film was about a robot becoming human. If he started out too human, there'd be no place to go, and the audience would not get to experience that evolution." Uncertain as to which approach was superior, Columbus decided to keep his options open by having XFX develop both a full robot suit and a robot makeup. So crucial was the decision that even as shooting commenced, it remained unclear as to which direction Columbus would steer the project. "Chris never made any bones about the fact that if the robot didn't work, his movie didn't work," said Johnson. "So we were all nervous wrecks. Up until a week into shooting, Chris still hadn't decided if the robot suit would work, and we didn't know for sure if it would even be in the movie." Design work for both makeup and suit versions of Andrew had begun nine months prior to the start of filming, with concept illustrators Carlos Huante and Constantine Sekeris contributing countless sketches. One of the design imperatives was that the robot appear warm, friendly and nonthreatening. "It couldn't be offensive or frightening at all," Johnson remarked, "but it was, after all, a robot, so we were coming up with all these Japanese-style, large-extremity designs that looked like giant toys. We were working like crazy, but we weren't getting a lot of positive feedback from Chris." A breakthrough came during a meeting with production designer Norman Reynolds. "Norman said to me: 'Don't think of Andrew as a robot. Think of him as an appliance, like a vacuum cleaner or a blender. And that completely changed our approach. We started again, this time with the idea of Andrew as a very simple, utilitarian, multitask appliance in basic human form, but with things like bumpers on his feet so he wouldn't damage furniture. I started looking at Sharper Image catalogues, studying hip, cuttingedge designs for household items. There'd been a real revolution in those recently, due to the iMac. Suddenly, all these devices had translucent parts to them. So we thought we'd jump on the bandwagon, too, and make Andrew a giant, walking iMac." In keeping with that idea, the team designed translucent panels tinted to match the iMac's original blue-green color scheme - then ditched that coloration for fear it would seem dated by the time the movie was released. "As it turned out, it was dated when the movie came out," noted Johnson, "because by then, iMac had come up with other colors. We did stick with the idea of putting translucent panels on his thighs, back and head, but they were a more neutral color that blended with the rest of the suit." "Those wound up serving as maps," Johnson said, "but it wasn't until we prototyped the suit and built it that we really knew what we had." Johnson raised the stakes of the design chore by avoiding the obvious and more traditional techniques used in the past to create robot suits for the cinema. "I wanted to make a suit that didn't cheat," Johnson explained. "All the ones done in the pastlike those for C-3PO or RoboCop - have been cheats in that the areas of greatest mobility on the body were made out of soft material. RoboCop, for example, had enormous soft foam rubber areas around the arms, elbows, hands, torso, knees and ankles. I didn't want to do that. So we decided to construct the entire suit out of hard pieces. It still had to be flexible - we didn't want to limit Robin Williams' performance - but except for the palm of the hands, I dictated that there be no flexible pieces on the thing." The only way to provide flexibility and movement in the hard materials suit was to break it down into literally hundreds of mechanical joints and pieces. "There were a hundred pieces for the hand alone. It was a total nightmare, inventory-wise and production-wise, but all those small components made the suit move in a way that was really toylike and robotic." Before construction of the suit was begun, XFX did multiple full-body casts of Williams in various positions, from which full-size molds were made. The lifecasts confirmed what Johnson had foreseen as a possible difficulty - that any suit might appear too bulky and overly thick on the actor's stocky frame. "Robin has a barrel chest," Johnson related, "and he bikes a lot, so he has large, muscular thighs. So one of our biggest nightmares was finding ways to create a suit that was sufficiently streamlined. We drew attention away from the thicker areas by making those sections a slightly darker color, and by broadening the shoulders. We also stumbled on the fact that by making the feet a lot bigger and the lower part of the legs bigger, we could minimize the rest of the body. That finally made it work, and CINEFEX 81 • 15

Once Andrew's form had been sculpted, the XFX crew fashioned thousands of mechanical joints and vacuform plastic components, supported by a fiberglass understructure. The job was so extensive, it required 160 people working around the clock to complete it on time. Since the multipiece, hardmaterials robot suit was entirely unlike the soft, foam-rubber creatures XFX typically created, Johnson hired modelmakers to build it, reasoning that modelmakers would be more adept at dealing with the zero tolerances the intricate construct would most certainly require. "Building a monster suit is nothing compared to what we had to do to create this suit," Johnson stated. "It had to be engineered in a modelmaking kind of way, with pieces overlapping and sliding within each other, and ball-bearing units that could move certain areas. I just felt that modelmakers would be better suited to achieving that than typical creature makers." Vacuform pieces were cast out of transparent plastic, then painted on the inside rather than outside to impart a bit of translucence. The exterior of the completed suit was then matted to create a unique metallic finish. "On one of our first tests," recalled Johnson, "we matted down the suit, and it looked all right in person - nothing special. But on film it just glowed. It took on a velvety, bizarre alloy look, between metal and plastic, unlike anything that exists in the real world." Painting each separate piece of the suit proved too large a job to handle at the XFX facility, so an automotive painting booth was rented. "Once the color scheme was established," explained production coordinator Bob Newton, "we bought gallons and gallons of paint and started to work. We were vacuforming and creating pieces at the shop, then shuttling them back and forth to the spray booth. Each separate piece was fully painted so that there would never be an unpainted area exposed. The guys would create a thousand knuckle pieces, for example, and we would assemble them all on a board and send them over to the booth, where they would be painted individually." Facial movement was a critical concern. Initially, Columbus had requested mechanisms that would enable Williams himself to control the movements, creating a one-to-one relationship between the actor's real facial expressions and what was revealed on the animatronic face. But left with too little time to develop such a sophisticated system, XFX ultimately resorted to remote control mechanisms, conveying facial expression primarily through eyes and eyebrows, with an elevated panel on the back of the suit housing the motors that powered eye blinks and eyebrow movement. Williams donned the completed suit with each one-piece leg going on first, followed by the shoes. The pelvic area consisted of two pieces that bolted together in the front and back, as did the torso section. Each arm slid on separately and was bolted to the torso. The gloves went on next, followed by a bearing-capture arrangement at the wrist that was bolted together. Last were the separate neck pieces and the head, complete with hammered screen eyeballs that appeared opaque from the outside but allowed Williams to see out. With practice, the XFX crew got the suit-donning process down to twenty minutes. "It was actually less time than it would have been if Robin had been sitting for hair and makeup application," Johnson commented. Fans inside the head piece circulated air and helped to keep the actor cool and comfortable in the suit. "We had them on switches so that we could turn them on and off remotely," said Johnson, "and that really helped Robin. They were very tiny, since there wasn't much room in the head, but they did the job. We also put magnets along the hairline and in front of the ears and under the jaw so the face plate could be popped off between takes." While Williams himself was responsible for the suit's primary body, head and jaw movement, lead In his quest to become human, Andrew solicits the help of a renegade robotics engineer who has crafted a female robot with personality - another suit-based character designed and built by XFX. engineer Eric Fiedler, who designed all of the suit's animatronics, operated the remote-controlled facial functions from off-camera. "Andrew's performance was the product of a remarkably synchronized collaboration between Eric and Robin," said Johnson. "The two of them really meshed. They could literally second-guess what the other was going to do." Despite all the trepidation and debate regarding the feasibility of putting Williams in a full robot suit, by the end of the first week of shooting it had become abundantly clear that the decision was a wise one. "Robin put on the suit," Johnson recalled, "and the thing just came to life. Early on, the studio had considered putting someone other than Robin in the suit, since he wasn't going to be seen anyway. But we all realized as soon as we started shooting that having a performer as talented as Robin was crucial to the success of the suit. Robin has a lot of mime background - which was a great help to us because he had such tremendous control. He'd say, 'Let's do a take where the eyebrows go up a quarter inch and I cock my head to the left.' We'd do that; and it would create a whole new expression." Five hero suits were fashioned, in addition to multiple suits for stunts and background robots that would populate the film. "Originally," stated Johnson, "the movie was going to have a lot of different robots, so we were designing giant robots and tiny robots - a variety of things. But for budgetary reasons, they decided that all the other robots would look like Andrew or a female version - just different colors. That way, we could crank out copies of those two prototypes. We made a snowplow robot and a baseball player robot and rusted old robots sitting in junkyards - but they were all basically like Andrew." Having resolved the central dilemma of the suit, Columbus did not have to resort to his backup plan - which was to have Dream Quest Images, already signed on to produce the show's visual effects, step in to create a digital version of Andrew. Relieved of robot duty, the Dream Quest crew - under visual effects supervisor James E. Price and visual effects producer Erika Wangberg Burton - nevertheless had a slate of eighty shots to complete. Most dealt with creating or enhancing environments that reflected the movie's near- and distant-future settings. In the film's opening, for example, Andrew is delivered to the Martin home - a shot that featured an exterior view of an actual home in Northern California. To match the layout of the interior set, a façade was built onto the entrance to the structure. Due to the CINEFEX 81 • 21

home's age and fragility, however, adding a real roof to the practical extension was not feasible; hence, it fell to Dream Quest to add a digital version. "We shot the house in Vistavision," related Price, "then built a 3D roof using the texture of the real one to create a 3D matte painting for our model. We also had to track it in 3D since there was a push-in and tilt-down on the background plate." Following his introduction to the Martin family - whom he refers to as Sir, Ma'am, Miss and Little Miss - Andrew demonstrates his acumen by reciting the three laws of robotics, displayed in spectacular fashion via a projector that emerges from his head to produce a swirling holographic light show. XFX built a special pop-up robot head specifically for the action. "The top flap of the head opened," said Johnson, "and there was a spinning device in the center that rose and shot the three primary colors onto a mirror and out into the room." The holographic laws were created at Dream Quest by digital effects supervisor Dan DeLeeuw and his team, who worked closely with Chris Columbus to narrow down a look for the display. "Chris wanted a startling effect," Price said, "something audiences wouldn't necessarily expect. Five years ago a floppy, well-worn cowboy doll named Woody locked horns with a slick, new spaceman action figure named Buzz Lightyear - and a new medium was born. Toy Story, the first cinematic offspring of a landmark union between animation giant Walt Disney Pictures and digital frontrunner Pixar Animation Studio, marked the first time that a feature-length motion picture was achieved entirely through computer animation. More important, it was a masterful bit of entertainment and a bona fide boxoffice phenomenon. The triumph of that first joint effort was followed by a second, the even more technically accomplished A Bug's Life. But audiences worldwide yearned for another peek at the beguiling, come-to-life toys inhabiting Andy's room - and it was only a matter of time before a third Disney/Pixar collaboration would assure As Toy Story 2 began to take shape in the mind of John Lasseter, Pixar's celebrated resident filmmaker and the guiding force behind the first two films, at the forefront was a determination to avoid the pitfalls that doomed most sequels to obscurity. "Everything at Pixar is driven by the needs of the story," Lasseter explained, "and my feeling was that the only reason to do a sequel for Toy Story was if we came up with a really great storyline. We could still have everything people loved about the first film - the characters, the humor, the action, the heart - without copying the original. So that's what we set out to do." Inspiration for the second story came to the director one day while watching his young sons joyfully dismantle his office. "My boys are typical Lasseters in that they love toys," Lasseter recalled, "and they love to come to Daddy's office, which is filled with toys from floor to ceiling. My toys are collectibles, though, and some of them are really quite valuable because they're one-of-a-kind; so I'm always nervous, because the kids are like bulls in a china shop. One day, I started laughing to myself, thinking: 'John! What did you learn from Toy Story? Toys are put on this earth to be played with by children. That's what they want to do more than anything else in the world - not be put on some shelf like a museum piece." Out of that observation was born the central angst of Toy Story 2, in which an aging Woody - showing definite signs of wear and tear - falls into a funk when Andy heads off to camp without him. Through a series of mishaps, Woody lands in a yardsale bin and is stolen by local toy store proprietor Al McWhiggin, who covets the vintage doll as the 32 4 CINEFEX 81 long-sought-after item that will complete his rare collection of memorabilia from Woody's Roundup, a popular fifties-era television show built around the cowboy character. Locked in Al's apartment while the toynapper finalizes plans to sell the collection to a Japanese toy museum, Woody meets and befriends his former Roundup costars - trusty steed Bullseye, cowgirl Jessie and a mint condition, still-in-the-box Stinky Pete the Prospector. Meanwhile, back in Andy's room, Buzz and the familiar toy brigade of Mr. Potato Head, Slinky Dog, Rex and Hamm set out for misadventures in the big city on a mission to rescue their purloined pal. The rescue is nearly derailed, however, when Woody - fearful that Andy will one day outgrow and abandon him - temporarily casts his lot with the sterile, but secure collectibles. "One of the things that's different about this film," observed Lasseter, "is that it's one of the rare times that a sequel actually changes genre from the original. The first film was a buddy picture, and the second is kind of a rescue/coming-of-age story. In Toy Story, we celebrated Buzz and Woody as toys. Buzz Lightyear comes in thinking he's a real spaceman, then has to learn and accept that he's just a toy. In this film, we actually celebrate both Buzz and Woody for who they are - Buzz as this incredibly cool spaceman and Woody for his cowboy heritage." The novel story angle was enough to convince Tom Hanks and Tim Allen - the voices of Woody and Buzz in the original - to reprise their roles. Indeed, all of the vocal talent would be back, as would many of the creative leads at Pixar - among them Karen Robert Jackson, co-producing with newcomer Helene Plotkin, and screenwriter Andrew Stanton, who this time around would share screenplay credit with Rita Hsiao, Doug Chamberlin and Chris Webb. Also returning were Lee Unkrich and Ash Brannon, segueing into feature directing as co-helmers of the show along with Lasseter. Although the story ideas for a sequel were certainly solid enough to merit feature-length treatment, the original plan for Toy Story 2 called for a direct-to-video release - the standard for Disney animated sequels. While work proceeded on that basis during the project's initial year of development, by 1997 change was in the air. Disney executives, having seen a rough story reel of the show, were prepared to recant their traditional strategy, and - much to Lasseter's delight - the project was upgraded to feature film status, with plans for a full theatrical release. While the move translated into a more generous budget and expanded resources, it also meant that some aspects of the work completed would have to be scrapped to make way for the larger film format. Fortunately, Pixar had dedicated its post-Toy Story period to boosting organizational and technical capacities in preparation for A Bug's Life, and was able to leverage off of that show. Key breakthroughs such as new subdivision surface modeling tools, a refined 3D paint system and an improved illumination model had already laid a solid technological groundwork. "The leaps, both visually and technically, that we took as a studio from Toy Story to A Bug's Life were huge," Lasseter affirmed, "and Toy Story 2 benefited phenomenally from all that. Plus, every leaf, every tree, every pebble, every stick, every riverbed that was produced for Bug's, we could reuse if we wanted to. On the first Toy Story, we were very reluctant to take our characters outdoors - we did that in just a few instances - whereas in this film, it was like: 'Let 'em out! We've got a whole digital nursery at our disposal!*" In fact, Toy Story 2, while resurrecting all the familiar characters from the original, would venture into new territory, both literally and figuratively, taking the all-digital feature to a new plateau of technical and aesthetic achievement. "Our main goal, of course, was to make something visually compelling, something that satisfied the expectations of a more sophisticated audience, but still felt like Toy Story," observed supervising technical director Galyn Susman. "As filmmakers, one of the things we knew we needed to focus on was making our films more filmic. We were very proud of Toy Story; but we knew there were a lot of things about it that made it feel like a CG movie. Some of those things are inherent in the medium, and we enjoy using them; but some are really artifacts, and we wanted to work on those. Although we didn't want to break from the Toy Story feel, we also wanted to explore a more sophisticated use of camera techniques. On Toy Story, for example, everything was perfectly crisp. Selective focus was not something we really understood how to use as a storytelling tool. But Toy Story 2 is a completely different beast. We worked to develop better depth-of-field tools so we could do selective focus, rack focus and moving camera shots - essentially liberate the camera. In a sense, we were melding the best of live-action techniques with the best of animation." Responsibility for Toy Story 2's universe fell to modeling supervisor Eben Ostby. Models for all of the returning characters had to be brought up to speed, wherever possible, to meet the newer, more

"We've done at least one, maybe two generations of models since Toy Story," said Ostby, "and, in general, the improvements break down into two areas. One is that our newer models just look better - they're more complicated and they have more detail in them, particularly along edges and seams. Where on Toy Story we would have brutally sharp edges on a model, we could now soften those edges so they would light and carry shading better. The other area is technical. Wherever we could, we built models that were optimized so that the people using them could have the best interaction possible. We made the control structures that animators use a little bit more uniform and efficient from character to character or model to model." Although no substantive changes were made to either Woody or Buzz, Ostby and his team did incorporate facial upgrades that took advantage of the new subdivision surface technology introduced in A Bug's Life. "Subdivision surfaces are great for topologies that have branching structures, such as hands and faces," explained Ostby. "We didn't use that technology in Toy Story, even though the development work was done long ago, because at the time it hadn't been tested in a production environment. We were going down the familiar road of ruled surfaces such as NURBS and B-spline patches. But Tony Derose, in our software development group, changed all that. He helped us realize what a great modeling tool 'subdivs' are, and we ended up using them on all of our models. In Woody and Buzz, for example, subdivs allowed us to get much better control of certain facial areas - corners of the mouth, and eyes and nose. In the old models, there would be cracking in those areas if the animators exaggerated the expressions too much. But with the new ones they were able to get a much wider range of expression without any of those artifacts." Other improvements to the look of the models were the result of an overhaul of Pixar's shading and lighting technology - a year-long R&D effort undertaken during A Bug's Life that resulted in the creation of a new illumination model designed to more clearly define the finished characteristics of surfaces by the way they reflect light. "In Toy Story, the illumination model and basic shader starting CINEFEX 81 • 33

point was plastic," remarked shading supervisor Brad West. "You were always starting from plastic and trying to go somewhere else - which is fine if you're going for a plastic look. But that's not what we wanted. So we rewrote the shaders using this new illumination model, which gave us more subtle shading effects and more control of lighting. Then we thought, if we're rewriting the shaders, why not go back and fix some other things that bugged us. In the case of Woody, for example, his jeans in the first film sort of read as denim; but if you look really closely you can see that the weave in the material stretches and distorts in places - which is a fundamental problem with mapping textures onto geometry. That kind of thing instantly raises a flag that says 'CG. So we took this great new denim that was created for Stinky Pete by one of our shading TDs, Guido Quaroni, and put it on Woody. But then the stretching became worse, and we had to find a way to go back and smooth all that out so it looked like the denim was following the surface of the jeans. We did the same for Woody's shirt." Although toy and hard-surface models would piggyback on earlier technological gains, creation of Toy Story 2's humans demanded new solutions. Besides the return of established characters such 34 • CINEFEX 81 as Andy, Mom and baby sister Molly, the sequel had several new ones - chief among them Al McWhiggin. the toy collector whose abduction of Woody sets the stage for all that follows. McWhiggin was to be the picture's comic, villainous centerpiece - caricatured on certain levels, but astonishingly real in the details. "We put a lot of focus and R&D into the creation of humans on this film," stated Lasseter. "Humans are, by far, the most difficult thing for us to do; and though they worked well in Toy Story, we wanted them to be better. We had done quite a bit of research for Geri's Game, a short animated film we did after Toy Story, and some of that could be applied to the sequel." Technical work on Al, assigned a high priority, was begun early in the production, with associate technical director Larry Aupperle taking responsibility for much of the model articulation, and Michael Krummhoefener sculpting the geometry. Once again, subdivison surfaces proved invaluable in the model work. With so much riding on the ability of animators to create an expressive performance, Aupperle and modeling artist Paul Aichele loaded Al's head with some 150 fine-tune controls - far more than any other character. Facial articulation ran the gamut from eye and mouth movements to Among the new characters created for the sequel were Jessie, a spirited cowgirl doll, and Emperor Zurg, a formidable opponent for Buzz. such subtleties as nostril flares, ear rotation and movement of the blubber-flesh of Al's double chin. Additional controls on the character's clothing aided animators in achieving a kind of loosefabric feel to Al's untucked shirt. Improvements in the depiction of Al's skin were the result of revamped shading and painting tools - an effort overseen by technical lead Mitch Prater working in collaboration with shading supervisor Brad West and his team. "On Toy Story, we had a really complex model of skin based on a SIGGRAPH paper that described fourteen different layers and how each reacted to light," recalled West. "It was phenomenally complicated, and although we got some decent-looking images out of it, when we put it into a lit scene, it essentially looked like plastic. It was the world's most complicated plastic shader. So when we started work on Toy Story 2, we said: 'You know, we don't do this for anything else - we don't model all these specific layers. We just twiddle with the knobs until we get a result we like.' So that was our approach this time around. Mitch just stuck his face on the scanner. Then he let the stubble grow out on his chin and scanned that. Next he tried to isolate blotch areas. Finally, he generalized all that into a really complicated shader with great controls that produced interesting results once it was in the hands of our painters, who defined a full range of skin characteristics, from wrinkles, moles and freckles to pimples, veins and stubble." Developing hair for Al was also high on the technical agenda. In Toy Story, human characters had sported hairdos that were little more than caps moving uniformly over their heads. For the sequel, a substantial chunk of the R&D budget was given over to the creation of realistic-looking CG haira problem that has long vexed digital artists. The work proceeded on several fronts. One was the creation of a new hair primitive in the core of RenderMan to create a simplified description of hair that could be rendered expediently. "The hair primitive had actually been around for a while," noted Ostby. "We started using it on Bug's for grass and several other applications, but it hadn't been used a whole lot for hair. When we started to do the hair work on Toy Story 2, this is what we wanted to use because it was faster, better, cheaper - a more compact, efficient representation of hair." (continued on page 39)

In the introduction to his screenplay for Pitch Black, director David Twohy notes: "The creatures in Pitch Black are seldom seen at length. Rather, they are glimpsed, they are heard, they are felt. They are, really, the embodiment of your nocturnal fears: A howling coyote that jars you awake; the painting on the wall that comes to life when stared at too long; the sway of your bed just before the earthquake hits. Chimera of the night." That 'less is more' philosophy would drive every moment of the film, a part-science-fiction, parthorror story about a deep-space cargo vessel that crashes on a seemingly lifeless, perpetually sunscorched planet. When a solar eclipse brings forth vast numbers of nocturnal predators, the crash survivors are soon fighting for their lives against the beasts - a battle made all the more harrowing by the relentless darkness. The original screenplay, by Jim and Ken Wheat, had been at PolyGram Films for many years before being substantially rewritten by Twohy, who was brought onto the project by producer Tom Engelman on the strength of his work on Terminal Velocity and The Arrival. "I was aware of David's talents and his enthusiasm for science fiction," Engelman commented, "and felt that he was a good match for this material - especially given the themes that we wanted to evoke. It was not just about a fear of the dark, but the fear of being subjected to the worst of circumstances with the worst of people. Since David is a writer whose work was based on strong structure and strong characters, we thought he would be the right director. Part of what David wanted to do was create a movie where the frights were as much what you didn't see as what you did see." Those frights that would be seen, however, would be created through a slate of two hundred visual effects shots. Brought onto production to serve as visual effects supervisor was Peter Chiang, who had started his film career as a miniature and optical effects artist and now stood at the forefront of the digital revolution in England. Chiang's work on The Borrowers brought him to the attention of PolyGram, which engaged him to set up a digital effects department in Britain. Producing digital effects for Pitch Black would be the first major project for Double Negative, the resulting London-based studio. So that Double Negative might concentrate its efforts solely on creature animation, Chiang and visual effects producer Alex Hope brought in The Magic Camera Company, another London house, to realize other digital effects under the guidance of effects producer Angie Wills and digital effects 48 • CINEFEX 81 supervisor Angus Cameron. While the majority of the effects work would be realized in England, the film was shot in Australia, both at Warner Roadshow Studios and on location at Coober Pedy in the country's remote southern region. Shooting in Australia gained the production access to a less costly, yet thoroughly professional film crew, as well as to the unusual, dramatic vistas of the Australian desert - a region that, featuring neither vegetation nor signs of human habitation, was ideal for representing the forbidding planet. Los Angeles-based effects teams were also instrumental to completing the film. Hunter/Gratzner Industries and The Chandler Group provided miniature effects, while Patrick Tatopoulos conceptualized the alien predators, brought to life on set in Australia by John Cox, who produced animatronic puppets based on the Tatopoulos designs. Early preproduction work centered on conceiving the opening crash of the space freighter on the barren planet. The sequence was created by HGI, which was brought onto the show early enough to actually design the spaceship and storyboard the entire crash sequence. "We wanted to give the ship and the overall sequence a gritty feel," stated HGI partner lan Hunter. "Because this was the opening of the film, David wanted it to look like a documentary. To us, that suggested being close up and getting the visceral feel of things shaking and breaking apart in a physical environment with miniatures. We wanted those 'random acts of violence' that you don't get with CG unless you spend a lot of time animating them." The film's first shot reveals the 300-foot-long freighter in space. As designed by Hunter/Gratzner, the segmented craft was comprised of linked cargo containers sandwiched between a forward command section and an aft engine section. "Since the vessel was supposed to belong to a shipping company," HGI partner Matthew Gratzner reasoned, "it made sense that it would have interchangeable cargo containers. So we came up with a 'freight train in space' concept." Some elements of the design were driven by the practicalities of set construction. "The ship had to have a few aerodynamic properties - such as the rounded nose - since it was built for reentry. But the first unit was going to have to build at least some of the ship full-size on the crash site set, and the worst thing to give a set builder is something that has a lot of compound curves. They can build it, but it's expensive. Since the rounded nose of the ship would be destroyed in the crash anyway, they wouldn't have to build that; and we made sure that everything aft of that was faceted to make it more economical for them, and us, to construct. After we finalized the drawings, we built a foam maquette for the production to sign off on." At 1/36-scale, the hero spaceship model measured a little more than nine feet long and fourteen inches wide, with ten containers in two side-by-side rows along the length. Masters of the principal parts were cast, molded in epoxy fiberglass, then fitted around a rigid steel frame that featured motion control mounting points at the top, bottom and two sides. To create the look of metal panels, aluminum tape was applied to the model surfaces. Practical lights included white dorsal and ventral beacons and green and red navigation lights. "We fitted two bright krypton bulbs in each of the engines," said Hunter, "and in front of those we put etched-brass screen diffusers. Between the screens and the bulbs we placed layered blue and magenta gels. We also added a green-gelled light in the cockpit to suggest a glow from the instrument panel." Movable parts included stepper-driven wings, and extendable airbrakes in the front and back. Because the script had originally called for the film to open inside the ship - where damage from meteor hits has caused cryo-lockers containing the sleeping crew members to blow open - the introductory outer view of the freighter in space was a late addition in the production schedule. "For the new opening," stated Chiang, "the nine-foot model was shipped to England for a seventy-second motion control shot." Programmed and lit by Rick Mietkowski, the model was filmed against greenscreen and composited at Double Negative by Chris Panton, with a CGI comet created by Jim Bowers. Main titles were also laid into the shot, provided as Illustrator files by Pacific Title. Micrometeoroids are then revealed impacting and damaging the ship - an effect produced by The Magic Camera Company as highspeed, superheated vapor trails. With the captain killed in the sudden explosion of the cryo-lockers, the co-pilot takes the controls. Attempting to slow the damaged vessel by deploying its airbrakes - several of which tear away under the stress of passage through the remote planet's atmosphere - she jettisons cargo containers and other unnecessary sections of the ship. To accommodate the action, the hero ship miniature was designed and constructed so that it could be filmed as a whole first, then with various sections removed as the sequence progressed. When NASA's unmanned Viking probe touched down on the surface of Mars in 1976, it dispelled a century's-worth of speculation concerning life on the red planet. Soil tests indicated the strong likelihood that Mars was barren, dashing the hopes of many while rendering reams of science fiction stories obsolete. But interest remained high, as evidenced by the Internet mania surrounding images broadcast from the space probe Pathfinder in 1997, following its Mars landing, A website displaying the photos registered one hundred million hits in a single day. While the planet would appear to be a dead world, it remains within the realm of scientific possibility that Mars once teemed with life. Exploring this notion -and touching on others even more speculative about the origins of life in our solar system - Mission to Mars envisions mankind's ill-fated first expedition to its nearest planetary neighbor. An inexplicable force wipes out most of the crew, leaving as sole survivor mission commander Luke Graham (Don Cheadle), who must await rescue from earth. But the recovery mission - crewed by commander Woody Blake (Tim Robbins), his wife Terri Fisher (Connie Nielsen), mission specialist Phil Ohlmyer (Jerry O'Connell) and Jim McConnell (Gary Sinise) - is nearly as disastrous as the first one, its crew forced to evacuate the ship following a devastating meteoroid shower. Reuniting with Graham on the red planet surface, the survivors attempt to solve the mystery of an alien artifact found there - a mission that ultimately becomes a race against time as a massive approaching sandstorm threatens to obliterate any chance they have of returning home. Scenarist David S. Goyer - also on board as one of the film's co-producers - would devise the storyline in conjunction with producer Tom Jacobson. A number of screenplays, first by Jim and John Thomas, then Graham Yost and finally Ted Tally, were drafted before the movie eventually found its way into the production pipeline. Dream Quest Images was selected as principal effects house on the film, while Gore Verbinsky, fresh from Mouse Hunt, signed on to direct. When Verbinsky left the project partway through preproduction, Brian De Palma took over the helming duties just a few months prior to the commencement of principal photography. Shortly after De Palma's arrival, the movie's release date was moved up from summer to spring - a strategy due in no small part to the announcement of a rival Mars project being readied by Warner Brothers. "We suddenly found ourselves with four and a half months lopped off our schedule," Dream Quest visual effects producer Rae Griffith-Gagnon recalled. "At that point it became clear that additional vendors would have to be enlisted to complete the effects workload. Fortunately, Brian De Palma already had a relationship with ILM, from Mission: Impossible and Snake Eyes, and so they were brought onto the show." As the shot count continued to grow, escalating beyond the resources of both Dream Quest and Industrial Light & Magic to finish on time, Tippett Studio took on some overflow work from both houses, while Composite Image Systems was called upon to turn around dozens of composites. Second-unit director Eric Schwab, a longtime collaborator of De Palma's, would coordinate with Dream Quest to review and amend some critical early animatics, while associate producer Jacqui Lopez oversaw contributions by other vendors. Completing the effects contingent were KNB EFX Group, responsible for the film's makeup needs, TFX, which provided functioning practical vehicles for shots of Mars exploration, and Rainmaker Digital Pictures, which generated and composited elements for on-set playback. Extensive physical effects were overseen by Gary Elmendorf. The verisimilitude of Mission to Mars' visuals was driven in part by generous cooperation from NASA, as well as production designer Ed Verreaux's desire to utilize genuine projections of near-future space exploration as the jumping-off point for the film's look. "As a result of working with Carl Sagan on Contact, I was acquainted with The Planetary Society, which is involved in near-future space development," said Verreaux. "I contacted them and began compiling data on what has been worked out for possible future space travel to Mars. While we knew there would be some dramatic license taken in extrapolating certain aspects of such a mission, I thought that using the NASA projections as a departure point would ground the film in a reality base that audiences could believe in - like Apollo 13." Verreaux assembled a team of concept illustrators - many of them veterans of other genre projects - to visualize the movie's array of spacecraft, land vehicles, spacesuits and Martian terrain, as well as speculative extraterrestrial constructs. A major design issue was determining a way to represent various Martian landscapes as full-size sets. "We did a number of power-scouts through the Southwest, working through Arizona, then Utah," Verreaux recalled. "But Brian didn't like any of those locations, and was considering building the Mars sets on a soundstage." Economic considerations prompted the studio to suggest Canada as a filming site, but the lack of a sufficiently large stage was a stumbling block. "At that point we started thinking of shooting outdoors again, and we began looking at parking lots and empty foundries up there. Ten minutes from the Vancouver airport, next to a river, we located a huge hundred-acre sandlot atop a landfill that was ideal. We could use earthmoving equipment to push the sand around and make whatever kind of landscape was needed." Over the last decade, the near-simultaneous release of likethemed movies has become something of a tradition in Hollywood. The fiery forces of inner earth were plumbed in Dante's Peak and Volcano, for example, while Armageddon and Deep Impact, released within a month of each other, examined the cinematic possibilities of planet-killer asteroids. At century's end, a number of pictures leveraged off millennium fever and the angst associated with prognostications of Satan's return. Among these were Stigmata, The Ninth Gate, Bless the Child and the oft-delayed Lost Souls. But the highest-profile of the lot was End of Days. Produced by Beacon Communications and released by Universal Pictures, End of Days stars Arnold Schwarzenegger- in his first action-hero lead since True Lies - as Jericho Cane, a disillusioned ex-police officer who faces down the Fallen Angel to protect an innocent from becoming Satan's bride and to prevent the biblically prophesied end of days. Music video director Marcus Nispel was at the helm when End of Days visual effects producer Kurt Williams first came on the project in July 1998. Visual effects supervisor Eric Durst was brought on a month later-about ten weeks prior to the start of production. With budgetary and creative matters in dispute, Nispel was dismissed in September; and, with less than a month before the start of principal photography, Peter Hyams took over. "As it turned out," commented Williams, "Eric was a terrific choice as a visual effects supervisor for Peter. Peter was both the director and the director of photography, which kept him occupied virtually twenty-four hours a day throughout the shoot. So we were fortunate to have Eric, because Eric thinks like a director and has a lot to contribute. That was especially useful since Peter came on so late, and only had three to four weeks of prep for this movie." Surviving the turnover from Nispel to Hyams was Durst's and Williams' breakdown of the visual effects. "There were several discrete sequences," said Durst, "each with particular requirements, so the decision was made to divide them among three to five houses. Of course, at that point we didn't know that the 180 planned effects shots would eventually grow to 425." Among other effects, the breakdown called for both a physical and digital manifestation of the devil. Stan Winston Studio would design the beast and provide its on-set representation, while Rhythm & Hues - having recently absorbed VIFX, Hyams' previous effects company of choice- would be tapped to create the digital incarnation. Additional computer graphics work was handled by Todd-AO/Hollywood Digital West and Centropolis Effects, and KNB EFX Group provided a variety of makeup effects. Additionally, a bevy of on-set gags and blasts were engineered by special effects coordinators Thomas L. Fisher and Scott R. Fisher. The picture's effects-heavy third act - incorporating extensive use of motion control, miniatures and pyrotechnics - involved three distinct companies working in close coordination. The firebeast then erupts out of him and flows around the church before being pulled down into the ground. In the last shot, Jericho, miraculously healed, would leave the church with Christine. Dissatisfied with that patly happy ending, Hyams lobbied successfully for a different conclusion - one in which Jericho remains impaled on the sword and expires after the firebeast roars from his body. The flame washes over the church, heading to the rear of the building, then turns and sweeps up to pause in front of the impaled man before being sucked underground and presumably returned to hell. An array of practical elements - flame-thrower effects and pyro orchestrated by John Stirber- were used for the gross fire action flowing across the church. HGI's miniature was photographed in several passes - once without interactive light enhancement, then twice more with lightbar effects triggered on either side of the model. "We put propane burners on solenoids so they could be shot in series, racing along the interior," stated lan Hunter. "Rhythm & Hues did a split down the middle so the takes could be combined." The fredeast would underdo a lendthy development phase. "Peter had suggested that we see the entire beast on fire," DesJardin recalled, "so 3D digital artists Scott Giegler and Ivan DeWolf animated a version with wings out, completely engulfed in flame, which up until mid-August was the concept - it even turned up in a trailer for the movie. Giegler and DeWolf next created a version that essentially retained just the head of the creature. "They supplied 2D digital artists Sean McPherson and Sean Lee with colorful renders for the facial details. With Satan vanquished - presumably for the next thousand years - Jericho dies. But before expiring on the sword blade, he is rewarded with a vision of his wife and child, both appearing quite happy in some kind of afterlife. A tilt-up pullback move at the end of the sequence was added in post, necessitating another return to the church. "We couldn't dress the church at all this time," Eric Durst explained, "so it was a matter of putting a crane in there and shooting the move. Then Mitch Drain took the shot on. At first it had been intended that miniature debris would be composited into the cathedral tilt-up shot. However, when the elements could not be massaged to fit properly into the environment, the debris was created digitally instead. "Most of the elements that I needed to create were broken glass," remarked Sean Cunningham. "But the other aspect to the shot involved the church's center aisle, which was replaced with a CG version so we could control the lighting. We actually subtracted light, reducing the big nasty hot spot that had been in the middle of the aisle - as a result, the number of lighting artifacts seen in the plate was also reduced."

On the streets outside, throngs celebrate the coming of the new century by watching the commemorative New Year's Eve ball-drop. These shots required miniature and CG effects work to augment a location shoot. "We got some great plate images in New York of the 1999 celebration," Eric Durst observed, "but when we got to study the ball they used, it was something of a disappointment - for all the magnificence associated with an item of such iconic stature, this was really just a tiny little sphere with wires sticking out the backi Fortunately, for the year 2000 festivities, Waterford Crystal had been engaged to design a more elaborate ball. Distinguished by 188 facets that made up a geodesic sphere, the new ball was re-created for End of Days by HGI, which assembled the reproduction in quarterscale - about eighteen inches in diameter - from scaled-down faceted pieces produced by Laser Custom Designs. It then fell to the modelmakers to incorporate six hundred lights into the sphere's interior and another four hundred across its surface, with a sequencing box rigged to control multicolored flashing effects. The actual ball-drop was accomplished within an elaborate rack - designed by Scott Beverly and built by Seth Curlin, Forest Fischer and Brian Kelly Hahn - featuring stepper motors that drove the ball up and down a shaft. Centropolis handled compositing chores, adding an 'NY2K' logo and replacing yearold advertising images visible in frame. Released during a highly competitive Thanksgiving holiday, End of Days generated solid revenues at the boxoffice, demonstrating Arnold Schwarzenegger's continuing ability to open a picture. The film's opening weekend success helped to recoup the cost of one of the most expensive independently produced movies ever made. "Universal handled distribution," Eric Durst observed, "but it was Beacon's nickel on the line. They raised something like a hundred million dollars; and while that seems like a lot, it goes very quickly when working on this scale. With the number of effects shots more than doubling as things progressed, we were forced to proceed in as disciplined a way as possible. Fortunately, our small group of key people - from the producer on down - was stationed together on a single floor of one building, and that situation created a different dynamic from many studio films. Lines of communication were greatly improved by the close proximity of all parties, and this fostered a better sense of collaboration. It could be a viable approach for future productions." The story idea for Galaxy Quest was so high-concept, so inspired, so filled with comedic possibilities, it must have been one of the easiest sells in movie history. One can just imagine the initial pitch... "There's this group of actors, see, whose popular sci-fi television show was canceled ten years ago." "You mean like...?" "Yeah. And since then, they've been reduced to opening car dealerships and appearing at science fiction conventions. "You mean like...?" "Yeah. But then alien emissaries from a threatened planet come to earth, looking for their help, because these aliens believe the show was real, that the crew of the fictional starship was the real crew of a real starship. So these washed-up actors end up saving the aliens, with the help of their fans, who call themselves 'Questerians." "Questerians. Are those like...?" "Exactly." "Are there alien villains, too?" "With scales." "Ah..." "And tentacles." "Oooh... Could we get Tim Allen to play the captain?" "Uh, huh - with his shirt off." "Could we get Sigourney Weaver?" "Yиp." "With her shirt off?" "No... but with lots of cleavage." "Sold!" Though David Howard, who conceived the story, and Robert Gordon, who wrote the script with Howard, might deny that the project was launched quite so effortlessly, it is hard to imagine a more commercially appealing film concept. Under the confident direction of Dean Parisot, the DreamWorks production of Galaxy Quest would have everything - comedy, pathos, action, science-fiction-style spectacle and heart, delivered by a stellar cast that included not only Allen and Weaver, but Alan Rickman, Tony Shalhoub and Daryl Mitchell. The film even had visual effects clout on its side, with Industrial Light & Magic brought on board to provide many of the story's key fantasy elements, including all of the space shots and computer generated creature effects. Also pegged for the project was Stan Winston Studio, responsible for the alien design work and the production's on-set animatronic and makeup effects. And it did not hurt that DreamWorks co-chief Steven Spielberg stepped in from time to time to lend his design and story talents to the show. The movie begins, appropriately, at a science fiction convention where cast members of the long-defunct "Galaxy Quest" television show are making an appearance. While signing autographs, actor Jason Nesmith (Tim Allen), who starred as Commander Peter Quincy Taggart, is approached by a small band of convention-goers who claim to be Thermians from the Klaatu Nebula. Strange, pasty-skinned and wearing official "Galaxy Quest" uniforms, the Thermians are virtually indistinguishable from the thousands of fans attending the event, and Nesmith dismisses their urgent pleas for help. These are no overzealous 'Questerians, however. The Thermians are the real McCoy, aliens who have patterned their society - even their starship, the Protector - on television transmissions of the old "Galaxy Quest" show, which they have intercepted and taken at face value as 'historical documents. Operating under the misguided notion that Nesmith is Commander Taggart - an experienced starship captain - they transport him to their ship at the far end of the galaxy to stop the aggressions of Sarris, a lizard-like alien who, with the aid of his reptilian henchmen and a space-navigating warship, the Falcon, is intent upon the Thermians' destruction. In the process of battling Sarris and such bizarre creatures as blue demons, a pig lizard and a monster made of rock, Nesmith and the entire "Galaxy Quest" cast manage to find redemption, becoming heroes off-screen, as well as on. Just six months before principal photography was slated to begin, Industrial Light & Magic began preproduction on Galaxy Quest. Sharing visual effects supervisory duties on the project were Stefen Fangmeier and Bill George, while Kim Bromley was designated visual effects producer. At the time of ILM's initial involvement in the project, Harold Ramis had been enlisted to direct; but Ramis subsequently departed the project, leveling additional strain on the already truncated schedule. "We had started working with Harold regarding concepts and designs, and had participated in several meetings with him," recalled George. "Then there was a two- or three-week period in which the studio was searching for a replacement. During that time, we continued to work on designs, knowing full well they might be rejected when a new director was brought in." Eventually chosen to replace Ramis was Dean Parisot, whose feature directorial debut on the dark comedy Home Fries had so impressed Galaxy Quest producer Charles Neuwirth that he recommended him for the job. While Parisot occupied himself with script changes and casting issues in preparation for principal photography, another personnel shuffle was underway at ILM as Fangmeier departed to supervise the effects for Perfect Storm. That left co-supervisor Bill George, an eighteen-year ILM veteran, in charge. Under George, visual effects duties would be split between co-visual effects supervisor Ed Hirsh and visual effects associate supervisor Ben Snow, with Hirsh responsible for all of the miniature photography-featuring both the Protector and Falcon spaceships - while Snow supervised all of the CG effects, many of which called for alien creatures. Another key team member was art director Alex Jaeger, who came on board the show later in the schedule and was responsible for many design elements, as well as the creation of animatics. As far back as Ramis' involvement, design of the film's aliens and its two featured spaceships had been paramount in Industrial Light & Magic joined forces with director Dean Parisot on Galaxy Quest, an affectionate spoof of the Star Trek phenomenon, in which the cast of a long-ago canceled television show is recruited to save an alien race. Believing the show to be video documentation of a real starship and its heroic crew, the aliens - called 'Thermians'- have patterned their entire society on the series, even to the point of building a functional replica of its starship Protector. / The vessel would be featured in both the real world of the film and in vintage clips from the "Galaxy Quest" TV show. For the ship's real-world shots - which Parisot envisioned as sophisticated, rather than campy - the ILM modelshop fashioned a highly-detailed, eight-foot-long miniature. / Practical model supervisor Brian Gernand and chief modelmaker Grant Imahara at work on an intentionally less-detailed, three-foot-long Protector, used in clips from the television show. In the end, most of the alien designs would come from the Winston team, while the spaceship designs would evolve through contributions from DeScenna, ILM concept artist Eric Wrigley, Fangmeier and George. George was particularly prepared for the task, given that he had designed ships for various Star Trek features over the course of his career - and Galaxy Quest was clearly a takeoff on that venerated series. Featured in a half-dozen shots involving television clips from the series, as well as some eighty shots in the 'real world' of the film, the Thermian Protectorwas the most prominent of the two spaceships and would go through the most lengthy and arduous design period. "The design process for the Protector was similar to that of the original Enterprise on the Star Trek television series," George related. "There were hundreds and hundreds of sketches done." Since legal concerns mandated that Galaxy Quest designs suggest rather than imitate Star Trek's well-established visual aesthetic, the designers of the Protector made sure they did not borrow too heavily from the Enterprise. "That was a serious consideration. In fact, there is a code painted on the Protector-'NTE 3120' - and that stood for 'Not the Enterprise. We certainly used the Enterprise as inspiration, but we also wanted something that was distinctive. What we wound up with was a ship that differed shape-wise, but had a similar paint job. It was more style than actual form and structure replication - which seemed a good compromise. Of course, it was inevitable that there be some similarities, because so many of the people on this show, including myself, had worked on Star Trek, too." The hundreds of Protector design sketches were eventually honed down to a few, with Harold Ramis - who was still on the film at the time - and Steven Spielberg making the final picks. Dean Parisot, his directorial ego remarkably in check, subsequently approved the established Protector concept upon joining the show. Such was not the case with the Falcon, however, the design of which was altered considerably with Parisot's arrival. "Dean wasn't happy with the look of Sarris' ship," George recalled. "He wanted it to be a bit more alien, more strange. He also wanted to suggest sea creatures in both the design of the ship and of Sarris." Another design imperative was that the falcon be distinguishable from the Protector. "We really wanted to get across the idea of a difference between the Thermian technology and Sarris' technology. Sarris' ship was supposed to be more primitive. The Thermians shoot lasers, for example, but Sarris shoots missiles. So the Falcon had to look more lowtech." Ultimately, the design of the ship was done by the production art department in Los Angeles. "They did a sketch and we based our model on that." With regard to the creature designs, Parisot's mandate was that the real world creations be credible, despite the fact that the film was essentially a comic parody. "People got in trouble if they used the word 'cheesy," said George. "Dean didn't want the designs to be cheesy. He wanted them to be absolutely real because, in the story, these characters are put into a situation that is real. He wanted a real sense of danger to be there." Among the 'non-cheesy' creatures were the blue demon children, cannibalistic inhabitants of a desert planet the "Galaxy Quest" actors visit in search of beryllium spheres to repair the damaged Thermian starship after a battle with Sarris. While the design of the blue demons originated at Stan Winston Studio, ILM refined the concept slightly in order to emphasize the tiny creatures' childlike qualities, while playing down the 'monster' aspect. "In the film, the crew is initially taken with these sweetlooking creatures - until they see them transform into hideous demons," commented George. "If you start with them looking scary, you miss that joke. So while Stan's work was mostly toward the demon side, ours was mostly toward the baby side." Referencing Photoshop artwork that incorporated photographs of real babies, ILM artists made subtle changes to the Winston designs. "Stan's version had a pointy tail, for example, and we took the tail off. We also made the creature a little plumper, a little rounder, and changed the proportion of the head to make it cuter. The biggest change was in the ears. To suggest that the blue demon babies are always listening for the rock monster - which shows up a little later in the movie - we gave them bigger ears that were constantly moving and alert, like a cat's ears. Those ears became a big part of the characters once we got to animating them." Nesmith, stranded alone on the planet, comes under attack from the blue demon hordes. Rendered unconscious, he awakens later to find that the creatures have inexplicably disappeared. But their absence is explained when the ground begins to rumble and boulders coalesce to form a giant, ambulatory rock monster. Nailing down a concept for the rock monster was one of the show's most difficult design tasks. "When we started doing drawings for the rock monster," George recalled, "people were very literal - they just drew a rock man, which looked like a guy in a rock suit. But both Stefen and I thought that wasn't the right approach. You have to come up with a theory of what makes a creature tick before you can design it - and in this instance, our theory was that it wasn't a monster made of rocks, but rather an entity and energy force that gathers rocks to create a body for itself. Our inspiration was Forbidden Planet and the 'Id' creature, which was basically a ghost. We wanted our rock monster to be as abstract as that - not to have a head and a nose and two eyes, but just be this big moving thing." As designs for all the creatures and ships took final shape, ILM turned its attention to creating animatics for each of the film's space sequences, in order to facilitate the choreographing of complex camera moves. Low-rez 3D animatics were created on a Macintosh, using Electric Image. "We'd work from the

storyboards that Dean had approved," George noted, "and we'd make sure we did that storyboarded version of a shot in the animatics - but I would present alternate versions, as well. Storyboard artists have a tendency to compose their boards with the spaceships too far away. These ships are supposed to be huge - at least the size of an aircraft carrier - and if you were really filming them, you wouldn't travel half a mile away to get them all in frame. I always approached the animatics with that point of view - if it were real, where would you put the camera? Fortunately, Dean is the type of director who wants what's best for the film; if he saw something that wasn't approved by production but was better, he would go for it - which was great." While the animatics team worked out space sequences in the computer, ILM modelmakers - under the direction of Brian Gernand - began building the practical ship models. Two versions of the Protector were built - a smaller and less-detailed model that would be used in clips from the television show, and an eight-foot version that would represent the Thermians' realworld ship. Working from concept art generated by production artists and the ILM art department, Gernand and visual concept designer John Goodson first built a twelve-inch-long Protector maquette for modelers to use as reference. The smaller version of the Protector afforded Gernand and his crew an opportunity to work out design issues and determine how the various parts of the ship would integrate, before moving on to the bigger model. Measuring just three feet long, the 'television' Protector's small size and minimalist detailing were a deliberate attempt on the part of the modeling crew to produce something that would look like a miniature on screen. "We left out all the classic tricks that we usually do to make a model seem real," explained Gernand. "It's not supposed to be the worst thing you've ever seen, but we didn't want audiences to confuse it with the real Protector. So we did as little as we could get away with and still keep it fairly decent-looking." The eight-foot-long, 1/200-scale Protector was fashioned to far more exacting standards. "A lot of the pieces were laser-cut," noted Gernand, "including the forward engines and all of the windows. Bryan Dewe was instrumental in helping us work out some 3D designs for the wings, and our computer-controlled laser-cutting equipment allowed us to generate left and right wings that were identical." Lightweight materials, similar to those employed in aircraft manufacturing, were used to construct the wings so they did not sag or flop when cantilevered off the fragile risers projecting from the ship's hull. The hull itself was sculpted out of urethane foam, coated with a polyester and given the standard molding and casting treatment. A spiny back and a command module - later seen separating from the big ship - were also built out of urethanes and vacuformed patterns. Hundreds of fluorescent, neon and LED lights simulated exterior and interior illumination. "A computer-controlled LED light gag rigged in the forward engines allowed us to program in a sequence of lights that added a lot of life to the ship. Once we got all the castings back, we opened up the ship and built our armature, then put in all the lighting and windows." After the ship was assembled and painted, UV paint touches were added to the corners of each of the scales at the overlap points, which, when illuminated with ultraviolet light, added an eerie glow to the already sinister-looking craft. "We tried to make it look as if the ship's interior lights were spilling out from under the scales," said Gernand, "which was a challenge because we had to work in complete darkness with just the UV lights on in order to see what the UV paint was doing." Fifty shots of the Protector and thirty of the Falcon were captured on the motion control stage, the models photographed against bluescreen by Sweeney and motion control cameraman Carl Miller. These shots would later be inserted into computer generated backgrounds. While the animatics served as crucial reference throughout the motion control shoot, both Hirsh and Sweeney were allowed some flexibility if inspiration hit -and it often did. "Probably 100% of the time," stated Hirsh, " we made some subtle change from the animatic to the actual shot. You can never plan those things exactly. Even simple things - such as the fact that the CG model in the animatics was shaped slightly different than the real model-made a big difference in the way we would frame a shot. Fortunately, we had all agreed from the beginning - and the director was behind us on this - that we could always change things a bit, as long as we kept the feel of the shot and stayed within the general time limits established for it." Since model photography elements of the ships in space had to be tracked and composited into digital starfields, efforts were made to accommodate that post task during the motion control shoot. "We kept a few of the Protector's running lights lit constantly," observed Brian Gernand, "so our matchmovers could utilize them as tracking markers. Traditionally on spaceship models, those running lights blink, synchronized to when the motion control camera is open or closed. But by keeping them on all the time, there were at least three points of light on the ship visible at any one time throughout the photography. It's one of those things that nobody is going to notice; but it made the matchmover's job a little easier." More conventional rules of model photography were broken in the shooting of the small Protector model that would be inserted into the "Galaxy Quest" television clips. Among the first elements to be shot, the model was lit flatly to make it look as low-budget as possible. "We also did simple camera moves that flew straight at us, then banked, with a little bit of a weave," remarked Hirsh, "whereas, when we shot the eight-foot Protector, we did much more complicated maneuvers." The low-tech look was enhanced when those model photography elements were composited against starfield backgrounds, with compositing supervisor Marshall Krasser adding such touches as film grain and scratches to the shots. "He even tracked in tiny wires holding the ship up," Bill George elaborated. "It was hilarious - but when Dean saw it, he said: 'Uh...no. You guys have gone too far.' So we pulled back from that. There were still visible matte lines, but we wound up with shots that were a little cleaner." Also captured on the motion control stage were shots for a sequence in which the Protector is seen scraping along the side of a gigantic space dock as one-time child actor Tommy Webber (Daryl Mitchell) gamely maneuvers the giant vessel out of the Thermian starport for a trial run. For those shots, the eightfoot Protector and a similarly-scaled miniature of the docking bay, built in the model shop, were filmed separately, then composited together. "We actually had two different versions of the docking bay that were built," said Hirsh. "One was a seventeenfoot section that we used for some interior shots on the bridge of the Protector, looking out, where you see the ship veering towards the wall. The other was an oversized section for a shot where we're very close to the side and we see it actually scraping." To ensure that the separately shot starship and docking bay elements would blend in the final composite, Pat Sweeney would program a move on the space dock, then translate that immediately to the model of the Protector that Carl Miller was filming on another area of the stage. "The two elements would then be roughly composited on stage, just to make sure everything was working together." Ultimately, one of our Rebel unit guys, Colie Wertz, modeled and texture-mapped the nose section, and it ended up looking absolutely beautiful."
