Space shots of the module separating from the Protector and reentering the atmosphere were filmed with a six-foot miniature provided by Gernand's team. For exterior ground shots of the out-of-control craft careening across the Paladium parking lot, compositors inserted footage of the module into plate photography of an empty parking lot, enhanced with CG cars and digital debris, heat ripple and distortion effects. Henry Preston supervised the 3D work on the sequence. Shots of the ship breaking through the walls of the Paladium and plowing into the convention center auditorium were executed with a fifth-scale command module nose section. Built by modelmakers Michael Lynch and Charlie Bailey, the model matched a full-size section used during live-action filming of the craft once it has come to a full stop. Also constructed was a detailed fifth-scale set piece replicating a section of the real convention center interior-with appropriate lighting, breakaway walls, floor, ceiling and stage, and set dressing. Though initial plans had called for a more elaborate crash scenario, budgetary constraints would require Hirsh to narrow the sequence to just three shots. "One was a shot looking into the corner as the craft breaks through the wall," Hirsh related, "another was a side-angle view as it travels through frame, and the third was a head-on shot as the ship hits the stage, breaks it apart, and comes to a stop." Filming of the sequence was accomplished with the module nose mounted on a hydraulic ram system, cable-driven on a track and sent crashing through the wall of the miniature set. Three locked-off cameras positioned on the other side captured the action at high speed. "We were prepared for five takes," recalled Gernand, "and we used all five of them. Each time we shot, we had to gather all the props and miniatures out of the rubble, clean them off, clear the entire set, and reset all of the breakaway pieces." Composited into the final mix was bluescreen footage of people running to get out of the path of the hurtling spacecraft and debris. As spacecraft elements were completed on the motion control stage, a digital team led by CG supervisor Dan Goldman and compositing supervisor Marshall Krasser began the work of inserting them into computer generated starfield backgrounds - created anew for Galaxy Quest, just as they had been for nearly every space show ILM had ever had a hand in. "We've been doing starfields at ILM for twenty-five years now," conceded Ben Snow, "but somehow we end up reinventing the wheel on every movie. Of course now that we're digital, we no longer use a motion control rig - we have software programs to generate them - but every visual effects supervisor wants his starfields to be the best that have ever been done." Digital artists started by going back to ILM's archives for reference purposes. "We looked at all these great movies we've " said Snow, "and some of the best star work is still found in The Empire Strikes Back. That's what we wanted to go for - a smaller type of star than is traditionally done in digital work. Bill George also wanted to add a radial galaxy arm so that you'd get some sense of geography in space. Plus, we wanted to push the look of the stars to give them a better, more organic scattering. So we really needed to extend the stars program; and Doug Applewhite and I actually did a lot of programming work on that. We had to go through the same cycle of tests that we've done in the past, but I'm convinced that now we have the answer - though it's already being enhanced a little bit for productions that are currently in-house." The film also called for the creation of starfields specifically for the vintage TV clips. These stars would have to appear much different than those generated for the 'real world' sequences. "We looked at Battlestar Gallactica and various TV shows - in particular, classic Star Trek- for reference," said Snow. "And of course, once again, they were all wildly different. On Star Trek they were pretty good, though. It looked as if they'd actually done multiple passes so that there were layers of stars." While the generation of starfields and compositing of model photography elements into those starfields would be a major concern throughout postproduction, modeling and animating of the film's computer generated creatures took up most of the post schedule. Some thirty-two shots would feature digital representations of the blue demon children. Using a Winston-built maquette as reference, and incorporating ILM's design refinements, digital creature model supervisor Geoff Campbell freesculpted the digital version of the blue demon's head utilizing proprietary software Isculpt, while Andrew Cawrse built up a library of face shapes for the creatures to vary the expressions. Organic-looking skins were created by Dan Goldman, who built

on technical advances in skin layering techniques derived from work done on Jar Jar Binks in The Phantom Menace. Animation of the demon children, under the direction of animation supervisor Chris Armstrong, required a subtle touch. "What made it difficult," noted Bill George, "was that this was a wacky comedy, but Dean was insisting the characters be taken seriously. So Chris and I tried really hard to make sure we got a subtle performance. I kept bringing up the example of prey animals in Africa at a watering hole. They're very afraid. We wanted the demon children to move like that - to seem like vulnerable animals, not little kewpie-doll characters." The blue demon children were composited into background plates of the planet surface, which were photographed in Utah at a stark desert park appropriately named Goblin Valley. For a big reveal of the crew walking through the alien environment, production requested a digital extension for the limited set area dressed on location. "It was a classic digital matte situation," observed Snow, "except that our painter, Ron Woodall - working with Jonathan Litt, who tech-directed the shot- ended up having to produce a lot of actual geometry, with backgrounds texture-mapped onto it." Digital compositor Mimi Abers was tasked with ensuring the demon babies were well-integrated into every background, be it digital or live-action. Abers enlisted the help of the rotoscope group to suggest interaction between the demons and water in the trough from which they drink, and added dust hits as the demons walk across the rocky landscape of the desert planet. Some of these additional elements were gleaned from an element database initiated by ILM during the company's work on Deep Impact. "We've been adding to it ever since," stated Snow, "and it's given us a big library of materials, both practical and digital, to draw from." Lighting the demon babies to accommodate the broad daylight scenario proved to be another challenging task. "Galaxy Quest was the first ILM production to use a new CG lighting tool we've been developing for some time - one that allows a much faster workflow," said Snow. "Dan Goldman put a tremendous amount of work into integrating this software successfully into our pipeline, and sequence supervisor Henry Preston worked with the tech directors to ensure consistency." Several shots required whole hordes of the creatures to pursue the humans as they scrambled back to their shuttle. "We had Doug Sutton adapt some of the crowd creation techniques that he helped develop for Phantom Menace. He and fellow TD David Parrish animated the demons as particles in Maya, using cycles developed by Chris Armstrong's animators that showed them walking, running, jumping and snarling. These were then inserted in place of the particles at render time." Figuring into some thirty to thirty-five shots on the planet, and later on board the Protector, was the rock monster, another difficult undertaking for the modeling, animation and compositing teams. ation, the tight postproduction schedule left no time for tests or animatics. "We had artwork, but it was static," George noted, "so we were working on nothing but faith - faith that we could get this thing to work." Overseeing the rock monster creation was a core team consisting of sequence supervisor Ed Kramer, modeler Sonny Wei and lead animator Scott 'Huck' Wirtz, working with Softimage. "Though Bill George did the initial designs," remarked Snow, "the rock monster was transformed as Ed and Huck and Sonny worked together to figure out the dynamics of the thing. It went through quite an evolution. When it finally came together, it had two legs, two arms and a head, and moved very much like a human being. There were big rocks that defined the shape, and smaller ones that orbited around and bounced off." Procedural animation, set up by technical animator James Tooley, figured heavily in the dynamics of the creature. "The model had to be chained so that it could be animated traditionally when it was walking; but we needed to be able to free the chain and let the rocks run through independent simulations for other actions, such as the monster slamming into a wall or the rocks initially coming together. Software developer Jim Hourihan developed an internal tool we called 'Fred' that allowed us to do that. We could say: 'Okay, I want the control of the rock monster to be ninety percent what the animator does; but I want to be able to run a simulation to make sure the rocks don't interpenetrate." The tool also allowed for automatic collision detection and debris generation. "The whole thing was controllable procedurality. We had full control of the animation initially; then we'd run our procedural elements on it, still able to dictate how much of it was random and how much was controlled. After that, we'd go back into Softimage again. It removed a lot of the pain in that we didn't have to worry about all the mechanical stuff." Animators did worry, though, about how to telegraph the required degree of menace for the rock monster without benefit of traditional cues derived from facial expression. "Ultimately," Bill George noted, "that menace was suggested by the weight and mass of the creature, how it moved, and the sound effects. There were subtle things that helped, too. When it stomped its foot down on the ground, for example, there were cracks that webbed out and things falling off the leg. There was a real interaction between the creature and the ground." Several shots in the sequence involved actual physical interaction between Nesmith and the CG creature. On location, Tim Allen had been pulled along the ground by a stuntman for a shot of the rock monster dragging the character. But the action did not match up well to the rock monster animation, which required that Allen's character be lifted off the ground as well as dragged. The team ended up having to create a CG Tim Allen for the interactive sequences. "Though we had to paint out the real Tim Allen and replace him with our digital one," said Snow, "it was handy having the real Tim in the plate as reference." Just as she had for the blue demon scenes, Mimi Abersworking under Marshall Krasser- reconstructed backgrounds from the Goblin Valley plate photography for the rock monster sequence. Not only did many backgrounds require augmentation, but seven or eight had to be created from scratch. "Digital compositor Tom Rosseter stepped in to help with the synthetic backgrounds," Snow observed, "compositing in elements from other scenes. Even Bill George picked up a brush and painted a couple of backgrounds for us. Our digital matte team - principally Jett and Ronn Brown - also did a lot of sky paintings. While creatures and spaceships would occupy most of ILM's attention, Galaxy Quest featured a variety of visual effects that fell into neither category. The 'gelevator,' for example - whereby Nesmith, and later his cast mates, are propelled across the galaxy immersed head to toe in a protective, gelatinous goo - was more a challenge from an aesthetic standpoint than from a technical one. The gelevator is first revealed when Nesmith is transported home from the Thermian starport early in the film. "It was a simple concept to have this digital goo come up and cover his body," stated Bill George, "but to make it look as if he was really inside of it was difficult. Although the gel was supposedly holding him in place, he was moving slightly, trying to get out, so it had to jiggle in response. Our reference was Jell-o. Everyone knows how Jell-o moves - it's programmed into our brains - but it was difficult to nail that look." Technical director David Hisanaga ultimately created a goo that mimicked the look of Jell-o; but there remained the problem of suggesting real interaction between the subject and the digital covering. To resolve the dilemma, Sonny Wei produced a reasonably detailed model of Tim Allen, which modelers then encased in a digital sleeve that roughly matched the actor's movement, with the goo subsequently following the motion of the sleeve. "The goo had to be affected by his motions and wobble about," said Snow, "but it couldn't penetrate through. Otherwise we'd get shots where part of the actor's head was sticking out. So we took the sleeve into our Maya Dynamics system to work that out. Fortunately, Maya gave us enough control to get what we wanted; and it provided a kind of collision detection that kept parts of the actor from sticking out of the goo." Another challenge was embuing the essentially transparent substance with a sense of volume. "We used a lot of displacement and multiple layers of sleeves to really get a sense of volume. We even cheated the amount of reflection, just to give it interest, inserting more lights and reflections of more people than were actually on the set. Then we added 2D smoke elements, bubbles and some practical methocel drips we had shot." There were significant differences, however. "Unlike the transporter," said George, "which is all bubbly and soft so that you imagine it would be a pleasant experience, the digital conveyor was to look fast and painful. It's as if a hand comes down and yanks the character up from one place, then throws him back in the 25th Century featuring a transporter effect - which was basically like getting hit by lightning - and Dean just loved it. So we based ours on that." Development of the conveyor effect was principally the work of digital compositor Dorne Heubler, with Katharine Baird's paint and roto team contributing handdrawn lightning animation. The final illusion, which made use of motion blur, was enhanced with practical elements such as dust hits and smoke. As examples of weird alien technology, the transporters were nothing compared to the 'Omega 13,' a mystery machine built by the Thermians in replication of a similar device, of unspecified and indeterminate function, introduced on the television series. Several scenes would feature the nebulous Omega 13, including one in which Nesmith and Gwen DeMarco (Sigourney Weaver), on their way to disengage the Protector's neutron reactor so as to keep the ship from self-destructing, glimpse the effect from a walkway spanning a chasm. "Production wanted to convey the sense of an alien technology at work," remarked Snow, "so we did quite a lot of investigating into ways that we could convey that." The Omega 13 was eventually conceived as undulating blue blobs of energy trapped within a mesh-like cage, with tentacles wafting out of the core. With less than two months of postproduction remaining, Ben Snow worked with technical directors Hilmar Koch and Aron Bonar to realize the computer generated effect. "Aron created the inner and outer spheres in Maya with particle simulation," Snow explained. "In the first shot you just see the balls fairly static, as the tentacles - animated by Scott Wirtz - waft down towards the crew members. Aron wrote a program that took that animation and said, 'Okay, we want these spheres to follow that animation. They'd stick to it like glue -which is actually a concept we used on Twister. In this case, though, we needed to have them lag a bit so that they wouldn't remain locked to the tentacles. Aron set up some code in the controls that allowed them to follow a little behind, which gave it a more wafting, organic feel." Further simulation enabled the animators to agitate the balls in direct response to a pulse traveling up the tentacles. After some discussion, it was decided that the cage surrounding the energy spheres would be realized as a painted model. "At first, we couldn't figure out how we were going to model the cage. Then we decided to try just using paint. So we wound up with fairly simple 3D spheres, with Ron Woodall essentially painting the cage around them, and Hilmar creating the appropriate lighting."

As ILM was wrapping the Omega 13 effect in the final months of post, Mat Beck and his crew at Light Matters/Pixel Envy were rushing to complete an additional slate of approximately fifty shots. Included were those in the 'chompers' sequence, in which Nesmith and DeMarco find their access to the neutron reactor core blocked by a sequential array of heavy metallic columns that move like vertical and horizontal pistons. Though practical chompers had been rigged on a live corridor set, it was later decided that interaction between the actors and the real chompers would be too dangerous. As a result, the chompers had to be computer generated for every shot in the sequence but the final one in which both characters are safely through the menacing columns. At LM/PE, the digital chompers were modeled and animated by Colin Strause, then composited into shots of Tim Allen and Sigourney Weaver in the tunnel - sans the practical chompers. The actors had reacted to the nonexistent chompers, making their way in stops and starts through the tunnel on the basis of cues shouted from off-camera. "We choreographed the motion of the chompers to maximize the sense of peril in the scene," explained Mat Beck, "but at the same time, we had to time that action to the actors' movements, while matching their eyelines. To make the chompers look really heavy and powerful, Colin animated them to vibrate a bit as they hit - as if the impact was so forceful it made things shake a little. That, combined with the sound effects, really sold the effect." Custom shaders were developed to give the chompers their highly reflective, metallic sheen. "There were numerous layers of chompers," observed Beck, "each one recursively reflecting light on the ones around it. It reminded me of those exercises from the early days of CG, where there would be a CG ball and you'd model the reflections all around it. For this, we recorded all the light sources on the set, and reflected all of them in the CG chompers; so when you look at the shiny cylinder of a single chomper, you can see the entire corridor and all the other chompers reflected in it." Extensive rotoscoping was needed to place the actors in front of and behind the computer generated columns. "One of the rotoscoping challenges," remarked Beck, "was that Sigourney Weaver was wearing a blonde wig, which was the worst possible scenario. It took a lot of extra tweaking to really make it look as if she was in amongst these chompers. Rina Osamupa also needed to do some fancy 3D tracking, which required that we model the entire tunnel in CG; and ILM was a big help in getting drawings and measurements to us so that we could do that. To integrate the actors and chompers even more, we cast shadows on the actors as the chompers came down in front of them. All of these things were required to make the chompers look as if they were really in the scene." "Much of what we do is similar to what a live-action set dressing department does," observed Eisenmann, "except that we take it one step further in that we are also part carpenters, part set constructors and part graphic designers." Although the original Toy Story did not require a separate set dressing department, A Bug's Life had served as 'finishing school' for Eisenmann and his team. "Bug's Life involved a lot of set dressing because of the kind of shot composition needed for all the vegetation," remarked Eisenmann. "We had to really compose how that vegetation was going to look, because it was different in every shot. But A Bug's Life existed in a very confined universe - we had one main environment, and we could reuse that throughout the entire show. When it came to Toy Story 2, we had to create eighteen versions of that main set, all with the same complexity and the same believability. And unlike Bug's, where we got really good at coming up with a certain look for the vegetation or rules and parameters for how the ground debris would work, on Toy Story 2, we'd go from an interior like Andy's room to a vegetation sequence outside, or to a downtown or an airport. There was a huge cross-section of different kinds of vibrant sets to give the sense that this was a larger world in which the characters existed. And it was all stuff we'd never attempted before." Adding to the enormity of the task was the need to design on multiple scales in order to accommodate both toy and human perspectives. "There were vast environments that needed to be dressed down to the scale of pebbles on the ground and twigs and trash and debris," Eisenmann explained. "The front lawn of Andy's house, for example, had to have as much detail as the entire main set of Bug's because of the action involving the toys; yet we had to do it so that it looked good from Al's perspective when we shot at his scale, as well. That was a difficult task to master." Once again, set dressers piggybacked on tools and techniques developed for A Bug's Life. "The Woody reels from a blast of bad breath as he attempts to escape from his sleeping abductor, revealed in extreme, detail-packed closeup. lawns in Andy's neighborhood were a big challenge," remarked Eisenmann. "Originally we tried doing grass that was just a shader on a piece of ground, but that didn't provide enough subtle beauty. We didn't get the play of light that we got in Bug's Life. So then we did real geometry in order to get a lot of shadow and subtle light nuances that play on the ground and cast shadows on the curbs and the street." Of particular benefit was a paint process, developed by Don Schreiter and refined for Toy Story 2, that enabled set dressers to predetermine the dispersion and specific look of various random objects comprising the broad outdoor expanses. "We would take plans of a set and paint down density maps, controlling what kinds of objects got placed, the variances, the sizes and color ranges, and their whole dispersion in the field. We painted down rocks and trash, grass, other kinds of vegetation - and that really drove our natural world." Yet executing the pitch black of the title while also allowing enough of the action to be seen was one of the production's main challenges. To overcome the obvious difficulties of that scenario, the filmmakers sought to 'paint' with darkness as opposed to painting with light. Very dim ambient coronal light from the eclipse justified some low-level illumination, as did light from an aurora borealis and lighting instruments carried by the characters. The sightless alien predators use sonar to sense their environment, through audible clicks issued via organs at the ends of bony appendages on the sides of their heads. The perceived 'vision' created by the creatures' sonar would be revealed to the audience by way of computer animation - specifically, a combination of Flame sparks, Chalice and Cineon effects generated by Richard Bain. Aware of the alien thermal vision effect produced for the Predator movies, Chiang and his team determined to create an altogether new look. "We developed the idea of a layer of noise sent out from the creature and hitting a three-dimensional object," said Chiang. "The shape of the object extrudes out of the layer as it disappears, and you get a quick blast back as the animal receives the information. That is constantly updated so that you get a regeneration, resolving the image as it sends out waves of organic noise. The three-dimensional object that's extruded takes on the texture of the noise, and depending on the sort of resolution the animal gets by increasing the frequency of the clicks, its characteristics are revealed. Since it's just sound, it's shown as a very monochromatic image." Having to make their way from the crashed freighter to the skiff, the survivors surround themselves with protective illumination, using bottles of alcohol with rag wicks as torches. Water drops and splashes in the sequence were practical elements tracked in by the 2D team. As the movie draws to a close, Riddick takes command and lifts off in the now repaired skiff. The scene opens with an establishing view of the council building, created as a composite of miniature, bluescreen and CG elements. "Shooting an aerial plate in Washington D.C. would have made things a lot easier," Dan DeLeeuw said, "but there was some trouble getting permits for the helicopter, and the shot came to us. The first problem was figuring out where to put the building without demolishing important landmarks. We finally found a site opposite the Capitol Building - there were neighborhoods there that could feasibly be torn down in the future." Animatics were created by scanning a map of Washington and roughing out ideas based on Reynolds' designs. After building a mockup of the miniature council building, the futuristic Washington D.C. was laid out in the computer. "We got as much reference material as we could," related DeLeeuw, "including stills of the Capitol Building and images from the Library of Congress. Then we proceeded to build many of the buildings in 3D. The landmarks that were more in the background - such as the Washington Monument and the Lincoln Memorial - were just image-mapped on a card. With those 3D 152 4 CINEFEX 81 and 2D elements, we began to assemble the shot." Those elements worked in conjunction with a practical council building model filmed motion control on the Dream Quest stage. When Andrew's appeal is denied, the robot/man opts to trade the immortality of his machine-state for the bittersweet experience of growing old with Portia. As the movie comes to a close, the two are seen in extreme old age, lying side by side, watching a telecast in which the president of the World Legislative Council finally decrees that Andrew is, indeed, a man. Dream Quest composited council footage into the set's giant, curved viewscreen, designed by Reynolds to cover an entire wall. To create a high-resolution widescreen image, the council plates were filmed as separate tiles and pieced together. Dream Quest then inserted the assembled viewscreen footage into a greenscreen matte area on the set. "Chris Columbus wanted the viewscreen image to be perfectly crisp and undistorted," said Jamie Price. "A Cinerama approach was taken in order to get the extremely wide field of view without distortion and to retain enough resolution to keep the image sharp. The irony of the concept was great. We were borrowing a technology from fifty years ago to illustrate a technology two hundred years Views of futuristic Washington D.C., with models and matte painting elements composited into live plate photography, were created at Dream Quest. in the future." The extreme old-age makeups featured in the scene demanded multiple tests and refinements of the silicone prosthetics produced by Greg Cannom and Wes Wofford. "Our first test of Robin's old-age makeup," said Wofford, "was done from a lifecast of Robin that we got from Steve Johnson. We created a makeup meant to make him look about a hundred years old - although we pulled back from that a bit when production thought the character looked too old." Williams, who had donned foam latex for his stint as Mrs. Doubtfire, expressed amazement at the natural appearance and flexibility of the new silicone when the test makeup was applied. "He kept touching his face," Cannom recalled, "because he couldn't believe the difference. Foam shrinks and is very stiff, but this silicone was amazingly fleshy. It was so mobile, Robin could do anything in it. He could smile, open his mouth and make any expression. He could put his head down, and the neck area reacted like a real fleshy jowl - whereas that movement in a foam appliance would have made it buckle up in a very unrealistic way." Though Bicentennial Man certainly elevated the standard for cinematic robots, in the opinion of those who helped create the illusion of a cyborg turned man it was ultimately the human touch that made the character work. "We absolutely could not have done this film without Robin Williams,"said Steve Johnson. "This was a performance delivered under the worst of circumstances for an actor - his body and face, the very tools of his craft, covered in fiberglass and vacuformed plastic. But Robin did it wonderfully, and he did it without ever complaining. If it had been any other actor, we would never have gotten through it. In fact, any other actor of his stature would have been against wearing a suit at all, and would doubtless have pushed for a makeup approach from the start.
